topics.title: Section A: Introducing socialisation, culture and identity

outcomes.text: Explain the relative nature of culture, norms and values using cross-cultural material.
Distinguish subculture, high culture, popular culture, global culture and consumer culture.
Explain cultural diversity and cultural hybridity.
Define primary and secondary socialisation and link them to agencies of socialisation, as a lifelong process.
Explain the agencies of socialisation: family, peer group, media, religion, education and workplace, and the creation of identities.
Consider the implications of the nature/nurture debate for socialisation.
Distinguish formal agencies of social control (police, law, courts, government, military) from informal ones (family, peers, media, religion, education, workplace).
Explain how identities are created, including the influence of agencies of socialisation.
Explain aspects of identity: ethnicity, nationality, gender, social class, sexuality, age and disability, and how they intersect and change.
Explain hybrid identities.

topics.title: Section B Option 1: Families and relationships

outcomes.text: Describe nuclear, extended, lone parent, reconstituted and same-sex families and non-family households, and emerging types.
Explain trends over 30 years in marriage, divorce and cohabitation, and demographic changes in birth rate, family size, age at marriage, age of child-bearing and ageing population.
Explain family diversity by social class, ethnicity and sexuality.
Explain the ideology of the nuclear family and the views of functionalism, New Right, Marxism, feminism and postmodernism.
Debate the extent of family diversity in the contemporary UK.

Analyse roles and relationships between partners and how power is changing, including the domestic division of labour and the dark side of the family, using functionalist, Marxist and feminist approaches.
Analyse roles and relationships between parents and children, including the child-centred family, extended childhood and the ageing population, using feminist approaches.
Explain theoretical views of the role and formation of youth culture: functionalism, Marxism/neo-Marxism, feminism and postmodernism.
Relate subcultures to social class, gender, ethnicity and hybridity.
Describe delinquent, criminal, spectacular youth, anti-school subcultures and gangs, and emerging types.
Explain patterns and trends in youth deviance by social class, gender and ethnicity from official statistics.
Explain youth participation in deviant subcultures using functionalism/New Right, Marxism/neo-Marxism, interactionism and culture and identity.
Explain the media and youth deviance: deviance amplification, folk devils and moral panics.
Evaluate evidence of how ethnicity, gender, social class and age are represented in the media and how this is changing.
Explain representations using Marxism, neo-Marxism, pluralism, feminism and postmodernism, with postmodernism as a critique.
Explain direct, indirect and active audience theories: hypodermic syringe, two-step flow, cultural effects and uses and gratifications.
Explain the media's role in deviance amplification and moral panics.

units.title: H580/02 Researching and understanding social inequalities

topics.title: Section A: Research methods and researching social inequalities

outcomes.text: Explain positivism: patterns, trends, objectivity, value freedom and quantitative data.
Explain interpretivism: meanings, verstehen, rapport, subjectivity, researcher imposition, reflexivity and qualitative data.
Use validity, reliability, representativeness and generalisability evaluatively.
Explain factors influencing the choice of topic, aims, hypotheses and research questions.
Explain primary and secondary data, operationalisation, pilot studies, data collection, respondent validation, longitudinal studies and interpretation.
Explain the relationship between sociology and social policy.
Evaluate random, systematic, stratified, snowball, volunteer, opportunity, purposive and quota sampling.
Explain access and gatekeeping issues.
Explain the British Sociological Association's ethical principles and why they should be followed.
Evaluate questionnaires, structured interviews, official and non-official statistics and content analysis for researching inequalities.
Evaluate participant, non-participant, covert and overt observation, unstructured and semi-structured interviews and ethnography.
Distinguish quantitative and qualitative data, and mixed methods: triangulation and methodological pluralism.
Describe patterns and trends in inequality by social class, gender, ethnicity and age, including work and employment.
Explain how inequalities affect life chances using evidence from a range of areas of social life.
Explain inequality using functionalism, Marxism, Weberian, feminist and New Right theories and their distinctive concepts.

topics.title: Section A: Globalisation and the digital social world

outcomes.text: Explain problems in defining globalisation.

Explain developments in digital communication: digital revolution, global village, networked society, media convergence, social media, virtual communities and digital social networks, and the link to social capital.
Apply Marxism, feminism and postmodernism to digital communication.
Explain the impact of digital communication on identity, social inequalities (class, gender, age) and relationships, positive and negative.
Explain the impact on culture: conflict and change, cultural homogenisation and cultural defence or glocalisation.

topics.title: Section B Option 1: Crime and deviance

outcomes.text: Define crime, deviance, social order and social control, and explain the relativity and social construction of crime and deviance.
Evaluate official crime statistics, victim surveys and self-report studies.
Describe the social distribution of offending and victimisation by social class, gender, age and ethnicity.
Describe patterns of crime in a global context: global organised crime and green crime.
Explain crime and deviance using functionalism, Marxism, neo-Marxism, interactionism, realism, New Right, subcultural theories and feminism.
Evaluate left-wing policies: community crime prevention, restorative justice and structural change.
Evaluate right-wing policies: situational and environmental crime prevention, retributive justice and punitive control.
Explain functionalist, Marxist, liberal, social democratic, New Right and feminist views of the role of education.
Explain functionalist, Marxist and New Right views of the relationship between education and work, including vocationalism post-1988.
Describe differential achievement by social class, ethnicity and gender, and their interrelationship.
Describe global educational inequalities: gender apartheid and disparities in provision.
Explain achievement differences through inside and outside school factors and structural, material and cultural factors.
Apply functionalist, Marxist, interactionist, social democratic, feminist and New Right approaches to achievement.

subtopics.title: Changes in the UK education system

outcomes.text: Describe the diversity of educational provision and types of school.
Explain government policies from 1988 onwards, including vocational and work-based training.
Explain New Right and social democratic ideological influences on policy.
Evaluate the impact of policy on competition and choice, raising standards, and equality of opportunity.

topics.title: Section B Option 3: Religion, belief and faith

outcomes.text: Define religion, faith and belief.
Distinguish churches, denominations, sects, cults, new religious movements, new age movements and fundamentalism.
Evaluate measures of religious belief, religiosity, belief without belonging and vicarious religion.
Evaluate functionalist, Marxist, neo-Marxist, Weberian, feminist, phenomenological and postmodern views of religion's role.
Evaluate whether religion is a conservative force or a force for change, using functionalism, Marxism, neo-Marxism and Weberianism.
Describe patterns and trends in religion by social class, gender, ethnicity and age.
Explain religion in a global context: changes in and differences between societies in its significance.
Debate secularisation in relation to belief, practice and the power and influence of religion.
Compare pro-secularisation and anti-secularisation (including postmodern) theories.
Explain government policies on religious equality, discrimination and freedom.
